Below is an overview of the most common security features found in today’s banknotes, a brief note on how forgers tend to attack or imitate them, and very high-level suggestions for how you might simulate analogous effects in a strictly “mock” or educational setting.  Always keep prototypes clearly marked “SPECIMEN—NOT LEGAL TENDER,” and comply with your jurisdiction’s laws on reproduction of currency.

1. Substrate (Paper vs. Polymer)  
  • Official notes  
    – Cotton–linen blend (U.S., €) or biaxially oriented polymer (Australia, Canada, U.K.)  
    – Feels distinctively crisp or slightly plastic; resists tearing and aging.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Forgers use heavy-weight art papers or transparency film to mimic thickness.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Source a mid-weight textured art paper (e.g. 100 gsm cotton rag) or clear vellum.  
    – Label it prominently “EDUCATIONAL USE ONLY.”  

2. Watermarks and Tone-Variations  
  • Official notes  
    – Real watermarks are created in the paper mold by varying fiber density, visible by holding to light.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Scanned images lightly printed on tracing paper or manual cutting of layers to simulate “lighter” area.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Print a grayscale version of your image on thin tracing paper, then overlay it under your main note design and view against a lamp.  

3. Embedded Security Thread  
  • Official notes  
    – A metallic or polymer thread runs through the substrate, often micro-printed and sometimes windowed (visible intermittently).  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Forgers press a thin metallic strip into a slit of paper or print a “faux thread” graphic on top of the note.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Sandwich a narrow strip of polyester ribbon or holographic craft foil between two layers of your paper; secure edges with translucent tape.  

4. Intaglio (Raised) Printing  
  • Official notes  
    – Deep-etched steel plates press ink so that portraits and numerals feel raised to the touch.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Use relief or letterpress printing; some forgers over-ink image areas then heat-emboss lightly.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Print your design on a laser printer, sprinkle clear embossing powder on wet toner, then heat to raise the ink.  

5. Microprinting  
  • Official notes  
    – Lines of text or patterns so small they merge into a line to the naked eye but remain crisp under magnification.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – High-resolution scans combined with 1200 dpi+ inkjet or laser printers. Clumsy forgers lose sharpness.  
  • Educational sim  
    – In your layout software, drop a 4 pt Arial or tiny pattern (e.g. “§§§§§”) around borders; print at the highest dpi your printer allows.  

6. Color-Shifting (Optically Variable) Ink  
  • Official notes  
    – Special pigments that appear green from one angle, copper from another.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Some buy off-the-shelf color-shift craft paints or inks and brush small areas. Forgers rarely match the effect fully.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Use a hobbyist color-shift acrylic paint on a small numeral patch; practice brushing lightly so it’s semi-transparent.  

7. Holograms and Kinegrams  
  • Official notes  
    – Foil stripes or patches embossed with micro-holographic images that morph under tilt.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Purchase generic holographic foil stickers and cut them to shape. Detail is poor compared to mint-embossed foils.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Order craft holographic foil (e.g. from a stationery supplier), press with a simple manual laminator or embossing folder.  

8. Ultraviolet (UV) and Infrared (IR) Features  
  • Official notes  
    – Invisible UV-reactive fibers or inks that fluoresce under blacklight; some inks only reflect in IR scanners.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Forgeries may sprinkle minute fluorescent fibers into paper pulp or brush on UV ink pens.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Buy UV-reactive craft pens or inks; add a few “fibers” of fluorescent thread to a thin glue layer on the note.  

9. Tactile Marks for Accessibility  
  • Official notes  
    – Raised dots or lines help the visually impaired.  
  • How it’s attacked  
    – Forgers often ignore this feature or simulate it poorly with glued-on bumps.  
  • Educational sim  
    – Use a low-temp hot-glue gun or clear silicone caulk to add simple raised symbols in a corner.  

Putting It All Together  
  • Layout:  Use vector-based software (Illustrator, Inkscape) to assemble background guilloché, portraits, microtext.  
  • Printing:  A 1200 dpi+ laser printer will deliver crisper micro-lines than most inkjets.  
  • Assembly:  Layer your paper, inlays and foils; apply selective embossing/UV ink; trim and label “SPECIMEN.”  

Why Study These Methods?  
  – Awareness of how easy or hard certain features are to fake helps you prioritize what to inspect:  
     • Feel the paper and raised ink, tilt to spot color shifts, shine UV light, check thread windows.  
  – Understanding common shortcuts forgers take (flat holograms, poorly aligned threads, blurred microprint) sharpens detection.  
  – Mock-up exercises let trainees handle “counterfeits” without risking legal tender, so they learn to spot telltale signs.  

Legal and Ethical Reminder  
  • Always clearly mark reproductions as non-negotiable specimens.  
  • Never attempt to pass any reproduced note as genuine.  
  • Review local regulations—some countries restrict even educational reproductions of watermarks or UV inks.  

By combining a grounding in genuine banknote technology with hands-on mock-up exercises, you’ll gain both the theoretical and practical perspective needed to detect, investigate and prevent counterfeiting in the field.
